articles.title: Aditya-L1: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteries
articles.summary: Why is the Sun's corona millions of degrees hotter than its surface? And how does it maintain its inexplicably high temperature?
articles.body:
One of the most enduring mysteries that has been puzzling scientists forever is how the Sun's outer atmosphere - the corona - is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. And how does the corona continue to remain so hot despite frequent eruptions during which it loses huge amounts of energy?

Astrophysicists in India now say the latest findings from Aditya-L1 , the country's first solar observation mission in space, have provided them some vital clues to unlocking those mysteries. Their findings are revealed in a recent paper published in the prestigious Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physics, says leading Indian solar astrophysicist Prof R Ramesh of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) who led the study.

If you cut through the Sun's layers, deep inside is the core where the temperature is 15 million Celsius. Travel outwards to the surface or the photosphere - the part that we see from the Earth - it's about 5,500C. Far away from the core is the Sun's outermost layer or corona where the temperature is about 2 million C - it can sometimes go up to 40 million C.

Prof Ramesh says the corona is where extreme weather events - such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) - originate, during which large amounts of energy is released by the Sun into space. The CMEs cause beautiful auroras, and they can also affect life on Earth by causing geomagnetic storms that can knock down power grids and affect weather and communication satellites.

In normal or low-activity times, the Sun launches two to three CMEs a day. During the maximum solar activity cycle that comes every 11 years, there can be 10 or more in a single day.

"Now if the Sun is losing such huge amounts of energy with each CME and it's not replenished, the star at the centre of our solar system would lose all its energy and Earth would plunge into an irreversible deep freeze," Prof Ramesh says.

But since that's not happening, it means there's a "mechanism" by which the corona is able to maintain its inexplicably high temperature, he says.

Scientists put it down to two factors - one, the bubbling boiling motions on the Sun's surface that constantly generate waves which, as they travel outwards, carry energy to the corona - a bit like sea waves carrying foam and froth to the shore.

The second is the "tangled magnetic field lines" in the Sun's atmosphere that constantly snap and then reconnect. Prof Ramesh says a CME occurs when these twisting, looping lines - which resemble braided hair - rupture, throwing out massive clouds of magnetised plasma and gas in space. They often originate near sunspots, which are darker, cooler spots on the Sun where magnetic fields are particularly strong.

"But then these lines reconnect and the Sun replenishes the lost energy back within hours," he adds.

Why 2026 will be a year like no other for India's Sun mission

How important are India's Moon mission findings?

Why it costs India so little to reach the Moon and Mars

In their paper, Prof Ramesh says they have been able to quantify how much energy each of the two systems supply to the corona â which explains both why it's so many times hotter to begin with and how it retains that temperature after consistently losing energy.

Their study, he says, clearly shows that it's the second system that supplies most of the energy.

"Though the waves generated as a result of the bubbling, boiling motions on the Sun's surface generate and transport energy, their contribution is very little - they supply only 7% of the energy requirement.

"The remaining 93% comes because the Sun reconfigures itself and replenishes the lost energy."

To arrive at that calculation, Prof Ramesh says they studied a "very energetic" CME that took place on 5 August 2024. Emissions were recorded by Aditya-L1's coronagraph called Velc (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph).

"We saw that in 10 hours after the CME, the tangled field lines were able to go back to their original place, they reconnected and corona's energy was reconfigured," he said.

Chandrayaan-3: India makes historic landing near Moon's south pole

"We do recognise that energy generated by bubbly motions plays a major role in it, but we have evidence that it is not sufficient. Our study shows that the magnetic field lines snapping and reconnecting everywhere on the Sun are the primary source for supplying most of the energy."

These data, Prof Ramesh says, "provide an important benchmark" for future studies into the potential energy generation mechanisms in the Sun's atmosphere.

"I think they would help answer the fundamental questions of physics that defy logic," he says.

articles.title: Stolen Matisse artworks recovered by police in Brazil
articles.summary: A man is arrested after eight works by the French artist are found at a home in greater São Paulo.
articles.body:
Eight illustrations by French artist Henri Matisse that were stolen from a library in São Paulo have been recovered by police in Brazil.

The works, which have a combined estimated worth of about $200,000 (£148,000), were found on Thursday at a home in the town of São Bernardo do Campo, a suburb to the south of the city. A 44-year-old man was arrested at the scene.

During the heist at Biblioteca Mário de Andrade on 7 December last year, two thieves overpowered a security guard and an elderly couple who had been visiting the library, before making off with the artworks through the main entrance on foot.

Three other people were previously arrested in relation to the case.

Five engravings by the Brazilian artist Candido Portinari that were also taken during the robbery have not yet been recovered. Police in São Paulo said they suspected the works had been sold.

João Paulo Linhares de Araujo, the man arrested on Thursday, is suspected by police of having stored the Matisse artworks on behalf of those accused of being involved in the theft, as well as illegal possession of a firearm.

Laéssio Rodrigues de Oliveira, 53, described by Brazilian media as a prolific art thief, is suspected of having planned and directed the crime, according to Brazilian news outlet Globo.

He has been in custody since April after being arrested in relation to another case.

Another man and a woman have also been arrested over the library heist.

The Matisse illustrations, made for the limited-edition art book Jazz, along with five engravings by Portinari, created to illustrate a special edition of the novel Menino de engheno (Plantation Boy) by Brazilian writer José Lins do Rego, formed part of a joint exhibition with the São Paulo Museum of Modern Art.

The thieves targeted the exhibition, entitled From Book to Museum, on its final day.

They reportedly entered the library by its main entrance mid-morning and headed towards the nearest metro station following the heist.

Investigators said the theives placed the stolen artworks in a canvas bag to flee the scene.

The local department of culture said the illustrations had already been returned to the library, the security of which had been improved.

Matisse is widely considered to be one of the 20th Century's most influential artists and art critics say the value of the stolen works is "incalculable".

Portinari, who often painted rural workers and labourers, is one of the most significant Brazilian Modernist artists.

articles.title: People in Clacton react to Nigel Farage's by-election win
articles.summary: The Reform leader wins the by-election he triggered, and gains more votes than last time.
articles.body:
People in Clacton-on-Sea have woken up to the news that Nigel Farage will be returning to Westminster as their local MP.

The Reform UK leader secured 22,239 votes in the by-election he triggered by resigning in July, beating the 9,455 for second-placed Count Binface .

It was the culmination of a showdown in the Clacton constituency, which was boycotted by the other major British parties. Farage won more votes than he did when those parties stood against him at the 2024 general election, when he got 21,225 crosses on a much higher turnout of 58%, compared to 44% on Thursday.

However, a parliamentary investigation into Farage, who resigned the seat amid a row over his financial support, will now continue.

What do people in the Essex town make of the by-election result?

It was a "good result for Nigel", said Zak Apsey, but "it shouldn't really have needed to happen".

He argued the investigation into Farage was "not a big deal".

The Reform leader did not attend the result declaration, with his party saying the police had advised against it.

However, the BBC understands this was not the case.

"I wasn't disappointed he wasn't at the count. He was at his event, which is fine," Apsey added.

"He was still in the constituency, so what's the big deal?"

Jenny Hopkins, who made the trip to Clacton from Gloucestershire, said she was "delighted, absolutely thrilled" with the result.

"The fuss they've made about this so-called donation, gift or whatever it is - I think it is ridiculous," she said.

"This has proved the people of Clacton want Nigel Farage. However many by-elections they have, I think he'll win."

Linda Robinson felt the by-election was unnecessary and said she was not a fan of Farage.

"He's never here, is he? He's never in Clacton," she said.

She said that would be "all well and good" if her MP achieved great things for the town, but she said she did not believe he had.

Max Barrett was one of those people who voted for self-styled intergalactic space warrior Count Binface.

"It would be nice if he won, because it would be good for the area," Barrett said.

"There'd be a lot more tourism and it'd just be interesting him representing this area."

The Clacton resident said despite split opinions on the by-election, there were plenty of positives to take out of it.

"The whole community has come out. We're all talking to each other, which is very nice, no matter the difference in opinion," he said.

"We haven't had that for a very long time."

Some people in Clacton felt they were being used as part of a political "game", according to Sue Wackett, 70.

She felt let down by the Conservatives, Labour, the Liberal Democrats and Greens for not fielding candidates.

"It's got really nasty and for the first time in our lives, we try not to get involved in politics because it's scary," said Wackett.

"We need to all rethink and start thinking of each other as human beings, all entitled to our own opinions."

"I think the other parties were cowards not to stand," said Mary Williams, who travelled to Clacton from Wales to support Farage.

"They've tried to make it into a circus. They're all absolutely convinced he's going to be found guilty of something."

Pressure on Farage intensified after the Sunday Times reported he had not declared benefits , including staff and security, supplied with help from his long-term ally George Cottrell.

He has also faced questions about a £5m gift from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne in early 2024, which he did not register.

"I'm worried. I'm really concerned because I think Nigel Farage is the only answer, the only hope we've got in Great Britain," Williams added.

BBC East's political editor Andrew Sinclair has given his thoughts on how local issues have taken a backseat during this by-election campaign, unlike many other recent by-elections in the region.

articles.title: The execution of Leslie James, the last woman hanged in Wales
articles.summary: Leslie James was executed for murder, but her looks were talked about as much as her crime.
articles.body:
As Leslie James was marched to the gallows on the morning of her 40th birthday, she could never have known her death would put her name in the history books.

On 14 August 1907 at 08:00, James was led from the women's block of Cardiff Prison to a shed which housed the gallows, suspended above a 15ft-deep (4.5m) pit.

There waiting for her were Henry and Tom Pierrepoint - a surname synonymous with the noose - and with that pull of the lever, James would become the last woman to be hanged in Wales.

In June of that year, she was accused of deliberately smothering a day-old baby girl as part of what the police and press called a "baby farming" conspiracy.

But a new book by author Mary Jones casts doubt on details surrounding the case, highlighting James's previously unreported brain injury, and how her looks were as much the focus of the press attention as her crime.

In The Execution of Leslie James, Jones documents how in the months leading up to her crime, Leslie James, or Rhoda Willis as was probably her real name, was hit by a bike, giving her such severe concussion that she was in hospital for three months.

She argues: "Whatever Leslie's culpability in her crimes, this surely ought to have been taken into account."

James stood trial at the July 1907 Swansea Assizes accused of murdering baby Treasure, who was only identified by the surname of her mother, Maud Treasure from Fleur-de-lis in Caerphilly.

The prosecution claimed James responded to a newspaper advert asking for someone to take care of an unwanted baby, offering £6 initially, and a further £2 at a later date.

At the time, "baby farming", where "inconvenient" children were offered up for money, was seen as a social scandal.

After collecting the child, it was alleged that James smothered her on the train journey back to Cardiff, most likely around Llanishen.

Most damningly for James, evidence emerged that she had previously taken on two other babies in similar circumstances.

After a trial lasting one-and-a-half days, the all-male jury took just 12 minutes to convict her, in what must have seemed like an open-and-shut case in those days.

In passing sentence, the judge said: "Don't let anyone suppose that because you are convicted of murder that nobody pities you, nobody prays for you.

"I implore you to employ the short time that is left to you to prepare for death and for that mercy which you will undoubtedly find in heaven, but which you cannot expect here."

Jones believes there were serious flaws in the trial, most importantly that James's brain injury was not mentioned as an explanation for her reckless behaviour.

"Her barrister, Ivor Bowen, was only appointed on the morning of the trial on the judge's orders and, as such, there was no time to speak to Leslie or call any defence witnesses.

"Had they have done so, then the jury would have heard what baby Treasure's family told the police, that the child was already frothing from the mouth, possibly because of the indigestible sugar-water mix which they had given her because her mother was unable or unwilling to breastfeed her, and also that she had been extremely tightly swaddled, so that neighbours could not tell that the package being handed over to Leslie was a baby.

"Either of these could have led to baby Treasure choking or suffocating, though Leslie didn't help her own defence insofar as she was an alcoholic and, I believe, honestly couldn't recall how the infant died on that journey home."

Jones added that, while James's two previous forays into baby farming were used in evidence against her, the counter argument was never put forward.

She left a note requesting medical assistance for the first child, who she left on the steps of the Salvation Army, and the second was thriving after being adopted by her landlady, Mrs Wilson at 132 Portmanmoor Road in Splott, Cardiff.

On the evening of 3 June 1907 James returned home but couldn't sleep in her own bed, and instead bunked up with fellow lodger Rose Smith.

The following day she went out and got "paralytically drunk".

As Mrs Wilson tried to help her into bed, she discovered a tightly-wrapped parcel, which at first she thought to be a cut of meat, only to discover the truth and informed the police.

"She is most likely to have been born in Sunderland in 1863, though she claimed to have been educated in a London boarding school," said Jones, who believes there may be evidence to support this.

"Rhoda/Leslie appears from the records to have been a highly literate and articulate lady and far removed from the common-or-garden 'hussy' or 'fallen woman' which the press chose to stereotype such so-called baby farmers."

Jones said when James was arrested she gave her name as Leslie James, but on previous public documents she was variously listed as Rhoda Willis/Dalzell/Lascelles, daughter to a jeweller, Ernest Dalzell, which may have provided her with a more affluent background.

While living a "blameless life" prior to the bike accident, by 1907 she had fallen into "troubled ways".

She was locked in a love triangle with Scottish-born brothers Stewart and McGregor McPherson, between whom she bore two babies.

Jones said that by the time she sought lodgings at Portmanmoor Road, she was already deeply damaged.

"The way she sought shelter in Rose Smith's neighbouring room shows that she knew something terrible had happened, but it also lends evidence to the conclusion that she hadn't intended for it to happen.

"Surely, if Rhoda had have been guilty of murder, then she wouldn't have drawn such attention to herself."

Cardiff council, her own solicitor Harry Lloyd, and the general public raised a petition of about 50,000 names to spare her life.

A 1,000-strong crowd outside the prison were mortified when a guard pinned the notice of her death to the gates.

Home Secretary Herbert Gladstone had, the night before, concluded that she be made an example of because of the "despicable practice of baby farming prevalent in south Wales".

Jones said: "I am seeking an apology for the fact that such a troubled woman was hanged without evidence that she'd ever committed murder.

"It is beyond doubt that baby Treasure died while in the care of Rhoda, but her degree of culpability is very debatable, at the very most she is guilty of manslaughter."

Jones said a degree of misogynistic fetishism saw James go to the gallows.

"All the press reports and even the hangman Henry Pierrepoint remarked on her beauty and composure.

"No male's demeanour had ever been commented upon so much in the papers: 'From the way in which the sunlight caught her auburn hair to her composure at the moment the lever was pulled.'

"She was made to stand out for some sort of message."

Now, 119 years after she died, the only physical record of James's grave is an etched cross next to a potato patch within the walls of Cardiff Prison.

articles.title: Corey Ruiz funeral to be held in Madison after fatal police shooting
articles.summary: A 38-year-old Black man who was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin, was laid to rest Friday.
articles.body: A 38-year-old Black man who was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin, was laid to rest Friday. Corey Ruiz, 38, was fatally shot after he pulled out a knife in a struggle with four police officers last month, according to authorities. Bystander video of the incident went viral on social media, prompting a series of protests in the Midwestern city and drawing fresh scrutiny over the harsh police tactics used on the city’s people of color. The video of his death raised questions about why lethal force was used after Tasers were deployed. The funeral was attended by civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, who is representing Ruiz’s family, and the Rev. Al Sharpton, who delivered the eulogy. Relatives of Ruiz’s also spoke. His mother, Elsa Ruiz, said her son was homeless and treated like “he was just a piece of trash,” Wisconsin Public Radio reported. “He was not a piece of trash,” she said, according to WPR. “He was not a nobody. He was my son.” Before the open-casket funeral began, Sharpton told reporters that he came to Wisconsin after watching bystander video of the shooting, WPR reported. “This could be my brother,” Sharpton said. “This could be my nephew, and the fact that my name is Sharpton and their name is Ruiz means nothing to a cop that will unload and shoot multiple times, when they could have talked to him, they could have done multiple things.” Madison police say that on July 22, officers approached Ruiz after receiving calls reporting that someone was stealing bicycles and checking vehicle doors. Authorities said that after initially fleeing, Ruiz pulled out a knife during a struggle with officers and injured one of them. Officers said they tried but failed to shock Ruiz with a Taser before shooting him. As of Friday, no arrests have been made in connection with Ruiz’s death. When asked about potential arrests, a spokesperson for the Madison Police Department said in an email that “the investigation remains with DCI at this time,” referring to the Wisconsin Justice Department’s Division of Criminal Investigation. “DCI will then turn things over to the District Attorney’s office who will make a charging decision,” the spokesperson, Officer Stephanie Fryer, said. The Division of Criminal Investigation did not immediately return a request for comment. Ruiz’s case was not the first high-profile killing of a Black man at the hands of a police officer in Madison. Tony Robinson was fatally shot by police in 2015, roughly a block and a half from where Ruiz was killed. And in 2012, Paul Heenan was killed by a police officer nearby. Wisconsin public records show that Ruiz was convicted of 40 misdemeanors and felonies from 2009 to 2025, including robbery by force and strangulation. Ruiz’s ex-girlfriend, who is the mother of his teenage daughter, previously told NBC News that Ruiz struggled with mental health issues, but declined to provide specifics. She said he was killed blocks away from where his daughter lives. “She has to walk past his dying grounds and that memorial every day when she starts school,” she said. “Every day, she has to walk past that to get to school.”

articles.title: Anatel autoriza anti-spam e estuda levar sistema a todos os clientes | G1
articles.standfirst: Agência concluiu que não há elementos para considerar que ferramenta viole regras de concorrência, mas determinou que operadoras devem ser transparentes sobre critérios usados para bloquear chamadas.
articles.summary: Em disputa entre Vivo e TIM, agência concluiu que não há elementos para considerar que ferramenta viole regras de concorrência, mas determinou transparência.
articles.body:
O sistema da Vivo contra ligações indesejadas que foi alvo de reclamações da TIM foi autorizado pela Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações ( Anatel ), que avalia adotar bloqueios parecidos nas demais redes de telefonia. (veja mais ao final)

O chamado "Vivo Anti-spam" é tema de processos administrativos da Anatel desde o início de junho. A alegação de ao menos sete empresas, incluindo a TIM, é de que o serviço impede ligações legítimas e cria barreiras artificiais para concorrentes da Vivo.

Tem alguma sugestão de reportagem? Envie para o g1

Mas, na última quinta-feira (13), a Anatel concluiu que não há elementos suficientes para considerar o Vivo Anti-spam uma violação de regras do setor e determinou que a empresa pode continuar usando sua ferramenta.

A agência esclareceu que a medida não dá às operadoras liberdade irrestrita para bloquear chamadas . E disse que sistemas contra ligações indesejadas deve considerar fatores como proporcionalidade, transparência e igualdade no tratamento entre empresas.

Ligações automáticas indesejadas, chamadas de "robocalls" — Foto: Fantástico

Por que recebemos tantas ligações indesejadas? E como evitar esse tipo de chamada?

Um dos pontos questionados pela TIM foi a decisão da concorrente de ativar o anti-spam por padrão para todos os clientes – a ferramenta tinha sido lançada em novembro de 2024, mas só passou a ser ativada automaticamente em maio de 2026.

A Vivo disse que a taxa de cancelamento do serviço por usuários é de apenas 0,007%, o que reforçaria sua aceitação pelo público.

A Anatel concluiu que a ativação automática reduz a exposição de consumidores "hipervulneráveis" e com baixo letramento digital a golpes . Na avaliação da agência, eles teriam mais dificuldades para usar a ferramenta se tivessem que habilitá-la por conta própria.

Mas o órgão determinou que a página sobre o anti-spam no site da Vivo deve ter "informações claras, ostensivas e de fácil compreensão sobre seu funcionamento, incluindo os critérios e parâmetros utilizados para definir o tráfego sujeito à filtragem".

Além da TIM, outras empresas que questionaram o sistema relataram à Anatel casos de bloqueio de ligações consideradas legítimas, como aquelas feitas por serviços públicos de saúde, segurança e educação.

As operadoras também questionaram a falta de clareza sobre como o sistema define quais ligações seriam bloqueadas . Em alguns casos, os números foram liberados após contato com a Vivo.

A principal questão na disputa entre as empresas é o critério usado para bloquear as ligações, explicou Eduardo Tude, presidente da consultoria Teleco, ao g1 no início de agosto.

"O anti-spam do telefone funciona como o do e-mail: de vez em quando, caem coisas que não deveriam ter caído. Não existe um anti-spam perfeito que vai bloquear só o que deve", afirmou.

"A Vivo não pode bloquear as chamadas legítimas. A Anatel vai ter que estabelecer algum mecanismo para evitar que isso aconteça", continuou.

Anatel avalia ampliar bloqueios contra spam

Ainda em sua decisão, a Anatel recomendou que outros departamentos da agência avaliem a possível adoção de critérios de bloqueio de ligações indesejadas do Vivo Anti-spam pelas demais redes de telefonia.

Na avaliação da agência, o alto número de chamadas sem identificação e sem interação efetiva, como as ligações mudas, "configura prática abusiva, que deteriora a comunicação e promove crise de confiabilidade entre os usuários".

O objetivo com a recomendação é estimular a criação de padrões para barrar robôs no recebimento de chamadas, protegendo usuários que não saberiam configurar bloqueios manualmente.

Isso significa que o modelo da Vivo deixaria de ser uma iniciativa isolada para se tornar um padrão para todas as operadoras .

O órgão afirmou ainda que a padronização no setor ajudaria a garantir igualdade de condições entre as empresas, evitando que regras de filtragem fiquem restritas a apenas uma operadora.

Empresas afirmaram que sistema anti-spam da Vivo impediu ligações legítimas — Foto: Priscilla Du Preez/Unsplash

articles.title: 'O Assunto': veja como pais podem aumentar segurança digital de crianças e adolescentes em 7 dicas | G1
articles.standfirst: Especialista aconselha, principalmente, configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos.
articles.summary: Especialista aconselha, principalmente, configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos.
articles.body:
Pais e responsáveis podem adotar medidas para aumentar a segurança de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital, como configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos . As recomendações foram apresentadas pela jornalista Renata Cafardo no episódio desta sexta-feira (14) do podcast "O Assunto".

Renata é autora do livro "O algoritmo das famílias" e pesquisa a relação entre crianças, adolescentes, famílias e plataformas digitais.

Segundo ela, a supervisão dos responsáveis deve fazer parte da rotina familiar e ser adaptada à idade da criança ou do adolescente. Entenda as dicas:

1. Celular configurado com a idade correta

Uma das primeiras medidas recomendadas pela jornalista é verificar como o aparelho está configurado. Segundo Renata, o dispositivo deve estar associado à idade real da criança ou do adolescente, e não à de um adulto.

Isso permite que os recursos de proteção disponíveis no sistema sejam aplicados de acordo com a faixa etária. A configuração, porém, não é suficiente. Renata recomenda também o uso de controles parentais.

Os responsáveis podem utilizar ferramentas específicas ou recursos de controle parental disponíveis nos próprios sistemas operacionais.

Esses mecanismos permitem acompanhar a atividade digital e, em alguns casos, receber alertas sobre determinados conteúdos pesquisados ou acessados. Renata cita o aplicativo Qustodio , que ela afirma utilizar e recomendar.

Segundo a jornalista, a ferramenta pode enviar notificações aos responsáveis quando identifica pesquisas relacionadas a temas como violência, pornografia e saúde mental . Também é possível acompanhar pesquisas e vídeos acessados no YouTube.

3. Pais devem conhecer a senha do celular

Outra recomendação apresentada no podcast é que os responsáveis saibam a senha do celular usado pela criança ou pelo adolescente.

Para Renata, não deve existir uma expectativa de privacidade absoluta quando se trata de menores de idade e de um ambiente que pode oferecer riscos.

A supervisão, porém, deve ser explicada à criança. "Não é controlar, mas é supervisionar essa experiência digital", afirmou.

Segundo ela, os filhos precisam saber que o celular poderá ser acompanhado e entender que a medida tem como objetivo protegê-los.

Renata também recomenda que os responsáveis acompanhem periodicamente aplicativos usados pelos filhos, como o WhatsApp.

Ela defende que esse acompanhamento seja incorporado à rotina familiar, em vez de ocorrer apenas quando os pais desconfiam de alguma situação. A supervisão deve mudar conforme a idade.

Segundo a jornalista, crianças e adolescentes mais velhos podem conquistar gradualmente mais autonomia, mas ainda precisam saber que os responsáveis acompanham sua experiência digital .

Renata também alerta para o risco de transformar o celular em uma espécie de "babá digital". Segundo ela, se a família optar por permitir que a criança tenha um celular ou acesso a redes sociais, é necessário manter a supervisão.

A tecnologia, na avaliação da jornalista, não deve ser tratada apenas como uma forma de entretenimento que mantém a criança ocupada quando os pais não podem estar presentes.

Além dos controles tecnológicos, Renata destaca a importância da conversa dentro de casa.

Os responsáveis devem explicar os riscos existentes na internet de maneira adequada à idade da criança ou do adolescente. Ela compara a orientação sobre segurança digital a outras conversas que fazem parte da educação dos filhos, como aquelas sobre alimentação, bebidas alcoólicas, sexo seguro e outros riscos.

Para Renata, a tecnologia não pode ser tratada apenas como diversão. Você vai conversar sobre navegar no ambiente digital de maneira segura", afirmou.

A recomendação é que essa conversa seja frequente e acompanhe o desenvolvimento da criança.

Renata ressalta que a responsabilidade pela segurança digital de crianças e adolescentes não deve ser colocada exclusivamente sobre os pais.

Segundo ela, trata-se de um desafio de toda a sociedade, que precisa lidar com uma geração que já cresce conectada.

Ao mesmo tempo, os responsáveis precisam reconhecer que saber usar tecnologia não significa necessariamente ter maturidade emocional ou ética para lidar com ela.

Por isso, a combinação entre configuração adequada, controles parentais, acompanhamento e diálogo é apontada como uma forma de tornar a experiência digital de crianças e adolescentes mais segura .

articles.title: Who voted for Count Binface in the Clacton by-election and why?
articles.summary: Cheaper Flakes and using Adele to fund the NHS - voters on why they support a man dressed as a bin.
articles.body:
Self-styled intergalactic space warrior Count Binface finished second in the Clacton by-election on Thursday with 9,455 votes.

A record 34 candidates stood in the contest, but Binface and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage were the only contenders to secure more than 500 votes.

The other major UK parties boycotted the election, which was triggered by Farage's resignation as an MP in July, having won the seat from the Conservatives in 2024.

Binface has stood in various high-profile elections around the country in recent years. Before Clacton, his best results were more than 24,000 votes in the last two London mayoral elections.

With more candidates on the ballot than ever before, why did 26.9% of voters choose a man wearing a bin on his head?

First-time voter Ben Peters, 18, from Holland-on-Sea, said the election had been a "joke" since the start.

He said: "It was a bit of a thrill, but at the same time it felt almost pointless because I knew that, no matter what I did, Farage was going to get back into the seat."

Stephen Bear jailed over sex offender breaches

Has the by-election changed things for Clacton?

Anti-asylum protester who shoved police is jailed

Binface's policies had included nationalising the singer Adele, moving a pub hand dryer in Uxbridge and enforcing a 99p price tag on ice creams with 99 flakes.

Peters said: "Even if it means voting for Count Binface and getting 99p ice creams for 99 flakes, that is one more step than Nigel Farage has ever done for Clacton."

Alex Greenwood, from Thorpe-le-Soken, acknowledged some policies were "a bit silly" but the 18-year-old student argued there was an underlying logic to them.

"Nationalising Adele... all of Adele's song proceeds go to a private company which goes to shareholders and her songs are pretty much cultural icons," he said.

"It's not actually that far-fetched... why not have all that money go to the government which could be used on the NHS and stuff?"

Greenwood suggested his vote was partially a protest against Farage, whom he believes called the by-election to avoid scrutiny from the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards .

He added: "I do like Binface. I don't like Farage all that much."

Before Farage quit his Clacton seat in July, Parliament's standards watchdog had been investigating him for not declaring a £5m gift he received from billionaire Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne before he became an MP.

He said the by-election was a "people versus the establishment" showdown, saying the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions".

Kerry Mitchell, who lives in Wix, said she had voted for Count Binface because he would have made for a "more credible, honest, responsible, not to say committed, MP than Nigel Farage".

The 61-year-old, who voted Labour in 2024, said: "Nigel Farage poses a real threat to democracy in the UK and if Binface had won, it would have put an end to him.

"And it also added some much-needed humour and lightness into politics.

"The world is in a very dark place at the moment, and a bit of levity and humour is fantastic, especially when you contrast it with the rhetoric of outrage, division and anger that we hear from the far-right."

Tracey Donovan, 61, also voted Labour in the last general election and decided to back Binface on Thursday because it was "the only viable alternative to Farage".

"I detest Farage and everything he stands for. He has done absolutely nothing for our constituency," she told the BBC.

"I want an MP who represents our area with the constituents' interests being addressed.

"He claims the establishment is against him, but he is the establishment."

Donovan, who has lived in Clacton her entire life, added she was pleasantly surprised by how many people voted for Binface.

"He had almost a third of the votes cast as supposedly a joke candidate, and I'm very pleased that it is only really just over a quarter of the constituency [voting] population who actively backed Farage and Reform," she said.

"Count Binface could have rid this town of its Little Britain label if more of the 55% who didn't vote at all had got out there and voted against Farage."

Salon owner Verda Rigby, who lives in St Osyth, used to vote for the Conservatives before she "became a socialist" and started supporting Labour.

In this election, however, as voting for Labour was not an option, the 66-year-old instead opted for Binface.

"I could have stayed at home, but we fought for the right to vote and, look, it was partly for the joke that Farage is," she said.

"And I despise the right-wing parties Reform, Restore, and Reclaim - it's like a bad pop group of numpties."

People in Clacton react to Nigel Farage's re-election

Philip Bird, 66, has lived in Clacton for 30 years and said he, too, would have voted for Labour if the party had stood a candidate in the election.

"I think it was absolutely right not to stand anyone because none of the major parties should have condoned this election," he said.

"It was farcical, completely unnecessary, and designed to distract attention, and it wasn't going to change anything, so I was quite comfortable voting for a satirical candidate.

"Farage has greatly harmed the conversation in this country, he has been a dreadful MP, he has done nothing for Clacton, and in reality his politics are precisely what Clacton doesn't need."

In a statement after his win on Friday , the Reform leader said: "The verdict is now in, and it is a convincing, overwhelming win, with more votes than we got in the general election of 2024.

"Today, the voters in Clacton have stuck up two fingers to the entire political establishment."

articles.title: Solar eclipse in the South West: Pac-man to Shinto myths
articles.summary: Thousands turned out to watch the solar eclipse in the South West; here's what they made of it.
articles.body:
People across the South West gathered to watch a rare solar eclipse on Wednesday evening.

The event began at approx 19:00 BST with the Moon passing between the Earth and the Sun, creating a crescent shape in the sky.

In Sidmouth, families gathered to watch the event, with children describing it as a "once in a lifetime opportunity" and others comparing the shape of the Sun to a banana.

One young girl, Charlotte, said: "It's really exciting because the next time I'll see one, I'll be a lot older. It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity."

Charlie described the atmosphere as "magical", and said: "The kids haven't stopped screaming and been dancing around since we've been here."

Some people marked birthdays and anniversaries during the eclipse, giving the evening a romantic significance.

One young girl named Alice described the eclipse as brilliant, and said: "It kind of looks like Pac-man", whilst another felt that the sun disappearing was "kind of scary".

Commander Dave Lee, Royal Navy Parachute Display Team, spent the event parachuting into Pendennis Castle at the beginning of the eclipse.

Lee was one of five members of the Royal Navy and Royal Marines jumping out of the small aircraft at about 6,000ft (1829m), before deploying their colourful canopies.

Lee said: "It is really a once in a lifetime experience, you have a very real feeling of immediacy and freedom, and you get a great view."

David Heathfield spent the event telling stories about the "rare" mythology surrounding eclipses, in particular, the story of Amano-Iwato - the Japanese goddess of the sun - who hid in a cave depriving the world of light.

"I had to go all the way to Japanese Shinto mythology to find it", he said.

In Cornwall, people gathered at locations including Bude and a stone circle on the moors, with one person describing the experience as "very strange" and "surreal".

Another person said: "I think it's very, very spiritual."

In West Penwith, Mark said wildlife appeared to react to the changing light, with birds returning to their roosts as the eclipse took place.

"All the birds have gone to bed," he said, adding that a flock of seagulls and choughs had been feeding on flying ants shortly before they returned to the cliffs.

articles.title: ‘Revenge is inevitable’: Iran ramps up propaganda war with violent billboards
articles.summary: Anti-U.S. messaging has intensified since the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, with artificial intelligence playing a major role.
articles.body: The billboards are state-sponsored, plastered across Iran’s capital and far from subtle. One features an image of President Donald Trump lying in a casket; another shows the White House on fire; a third is a parody of the American flag with skulls in place of the stars and bombs dropping from the stripes. Alongside ads for a multitude of products such as cars and shampoo, the giant billboards have become familiar sights to the people of Tehran in recent years. But since the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an airstrike on the first day of the war launched by the United States and Israel, the messaging has become bolder and the tone more violent during the almost six-month conflict. Pictures of them captured by Iranian photojournalists over the last six months show people going about their daily lives next to the huge billboards with the violent imagery and messaging. One shows a busy intersection last month near Tehran’s central Enghelab Square, where a huge billboard featuring benign images of Khamenei was replaced with one of Trump lying in a casket, his hands together over his belly. In mock handwritten text, it refers to the sailors killed by a torpedo attack on the Iranian warship Iris Dena by the USS Charlotte attack submarine, along with a death threat aimed at Trump. Less than two weeks later, it was replaced by an image featuring Trump being strangled by several pairs of hands. “Revenge is inevitable,” a message in English said on it. A total of 17 U.S. service members have died since the start of the war with Iran, according to the latest figures issued by U.S. Central Command on July 18. On April 20, Iran’s semiofficial Mehr News Agency quoted Abbas Masjedi, the head of Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization, as saying that 3,375 people had been killed in the war. Anti-American rhetoric has long been a staple of Iran’s messaging since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and for more than three decades, a hand-painted mural parodying the Stars and Stripes has watched over passing traffic in the capital, Tehran. In place of the stars, skulls and bombs can be seen dropping from the stripes, which are emblazoned with the message “Down With The U.S.A.” across the middle. While that one is clearly painted, the more modern images appear to have been generated with the help of artificial intelligence, including one depicting the White House on fire. Written in Persian, the words “blood for blood” sit above the flames. Iran has used AI to boost its online propaganda efforts throughout the war, and one company, Explosive Media, has published dozens of Lego-inspired videos varying from short snippets to three-minute music videos mocking Trump and his administration. The company, whose work some have dubbed “slopaganda,” has told NBC News that it does not work for the Iranian government and that the government does not have a say in the content of its videos. Trump himself has posted plenty of AI-generated images, including some featuring Iran’s ships and energy infrastructure being blown up and taken over by the U.S. military.

articles.title: ‘I’ll settle for not crazy’: Denver business leaders brace for socialist shift after big win for DSA
articles.summary: Denver business owners react to the rise of socialist candidates and how their policies could shape the economic landscape in the Colorado capital.
articles.body: Affordability was a top concern among voters who helped launch democratic socialist congressional candidate Melat Kiros to victory in Denver's Democratic primary in June over 15-term incumbent Diana DeGette.  But as democratic socialists gain momentum in Colorado, business owners are grappling with how their progressive policies may collide with the actual costs of running a business in Denver. "With DSA specifically, I think that, too many times, the rhetoric sounds great until it meets the economic realities," J.J. Ament, president and CEO of the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce, told Fox News Digital.  COLORADO'S SOCIALIST SURGE SHAKES UP THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT "And, by the way, the basic laws of economics, they still apply even at altitude." Ament runs the oldest and largest chamber of commerce in Colorado, representing the business community. The chamber is nonpartisan and has members from both sides of the political spectrum, he said.  While the chamber does not endorse individual candidates, Ament noted that it does participate at the member level to promote pragmatic, pro-business candidates and promote free enterprise and free-market policies. "I tell people sort of as a joke, but not really, that I want pro-business. I'll settle for not crazy," he said. Colorado, according to Ament, has changed significantly over the past decade or more as the state has come under single-party Democratic control, shifting from one of the top 10 states for business to a place where increasing regulations and higher taxes have made it more difficult to operate a business. "Those risks could be created whether it's single-party controlled by Republicans or single-party controlled by Democrats," Ament said. "The reality is where everybody thinks the same, very little thinking actually occurs. And, so, the trend has been to more regulation, higher fees and taxes, the cost of doing business." He added that, as the city has grown and housing has not kept up, affordability has become a crucial issue, driving up the costs of running a business. GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS' As DSA-backed candidates took seats on the Denver City Council in 2023, the chamber warned that Colorado was becoming "increasingly hostile to business." Kiros' platform calls for a number of policies affecting the economy, including raising corporate taxes and the federal minimum wage. Ament believes some DSA-backed policies, like raising the minimum wage, have hurt the very workers and small businesses they were intended to help. "Just ask any restaurant owner in Denver how the government's interference in minimum wage and tipped wage has helped or hurt the very people, again, it was purported to be designed for," he said.  "A lot of times we have policies that are in the name of consumers, but aren't necessarily for consumers." Ament said the chamber's goal is to help people understand the economic realities of running a business while promoting policies and incentives that make starting a company simpler and less expensive. JOHN RICH WARNS NASHVILLE'S FAMED BROADWAY COULD GO DARK AS BUSINESSES FACE TAX ‘DEATH NAIL’ "We want every resident here to fully participate in the benefits that come with a thriving economy," he said. "But the choices that are being made are making that even more difficult. We were constantly trying to figure out how to create ladders to crawl over barriers when we just should stop creating the barrier in the first place." Brad Deen, service manager at Import Mechanics, knows full well the challenges facing small business owners in the area. He said his auto shop has faced increasing problems with crime, drug use and public safety as the population has boomed. "It seems like it's directly correlated to the influx of the population to Denver," Deen told Fox News Digital. "Seeing more unhoused and more open-air drug use than I would have in 2004." Deen was one of several business owners and residents who launched the South Broadway General Improvement District (GID) this year. Community members and businesses voted to impose an additional mill tax on themselves to fund private security and cleaning crews in order to make the area more appealing for customers. MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS Deen admitted he was reluctant to support additional taxes but felt it was necessary to protect his business. "As somebody who has kind of railed against tax increases my whole life, this was kind of a different line for me to take, but something that I felt had to be done," he said. He said the Broadway GID is already making a "huge positive change" by providing 24/7 staff to clean up graffiti and trash. The district has also worked to foster a more collaborative relationship with city leaders, and he noted that police have been more responsive and more present in patrolling the area than in years past. Deen took a pragmatic approach when considering how DSA policies might affect his business if Kiros wins the election in November. He said he has benefited and been hurt by policies from both the left and right and believes no one has all the answers to complex problems like homelessness. If Kiros is elected, he said he would ask her to address encampments outside Denver businesses first. EXPERT WHO FLED CUBA WARNS OF ‘VICIOUS CYCLE’ THAT WILL LEAD TO ‘COMMUNISTS IN DOUBLE DIGITS’ IN CONGRESS He expressed some concern about policies supporting higher taxes on corporations eventually being placed upon small businesses and hurting their operations. "As a relatively large employment group in the city, any large tax increases have a huge impact on us being able to, you know, get staff raises, give bonuses and provide benefits," Deen told Fox News Digital. Dealing with crime and rising costs is a challenge Jamie Sanchez, another Denver small-business owner, also faces. He runs The Drip Café in Denver's Santa Fe Art District. He also operates a Christian homeless ministry called Recycle God's Love, which he started with his late wife, Carolyn, in 2012. "I am seeing a lot of businesses turning over and shutting down just through the past three years we've been here," he told Fox News Digital.  "So, I could imagine why the cost of living here is skyrocketing. I mean, our minimum wage is insane right now to pay baristas to make coffee. So that makes it really difficult.  "So, I can only imagine, for some of the other business owners, it's getting really difficult, especially with rent and tax and all that going on. It's definitely been a strain on our business." Since opening his coffee shop three years ago, Sanchez said he has experienced broken windows, graffiti and threats. An outspoken Christian, Sanchez drew the ire of a local group called the Denver Communists before his shop even opened after the group noticed Recycle God's Love called homosexuality a sin in its beliefs section on its website.   Since then, on every first Friday of the month, protesters from the Denver Communists have held signs and passed out flyers accusing the coffee shop of being run by a "right-wing church" that hates the LGBTQ+ community. Sanchez said "Keep Santa Fe gay" and obscene stickers have also been placed on his windows and doors. "The Denver Communists specifically have targeted us because of the beliefs that we have," Sanchez told Fox News Digital. "Even though we haven't shown any hate towards these individuals. In fact, we serve people from this group at our homeless outreach.  "We serve them in our café. We've welcomed them in. We have invited them in. And, so, our goal is to actually show them the love of God because, yeah, we do believe different things, but our approach is to love them in hopes that they would come to Christ." The Christian shop owner sees the backlash as part of a spiritual battle. "The reason I come to that conclusion is because a lot of these protesters claim to be Satanists," he told Fox News Digital, adding that he's seen protesters wearing shirts depicting Satan or attacking Jesus. Sanchez said he now holds live worship music in the café every first Friday to help "drown out" the commotion outside. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "These groups have decided to twist things and use half-truths to try to stir people in the community to not frequent our coffee shop in hopes that we would not have enough sales to meet rent and that we will shut down," Sanchez said. "And it hasn't been working. In fact, the opposite has been happening to where people are knowing we're here now because of this situation and God has been using it for good." The Denver Communists told Fox News Digital they were not protesting the café strictly because it is Christian, but because of its religious beliefs about sexuality. "We are not targeting Christianity. We [are] targeting homophobia and transphobia," a spokesperson for the Denver Communists said. "Sanchez wants to claim Drip’s particular right-wing evangelical fundamentalism is representative of all Christianity, but it’s not. Many Christians are not homophobes and transphobes. Many Christians have joined us in protesting against Drip, including clergy members." The group, which formed in 2012 as a branch of the International Socialist Organization, told Fox News Digital it views the Drip Café's mission as part of a nationwide, right-wing "coordinated assault ... against the democratic rights and cultural acceptance won by LGBTQ+ people." "Right-wing churches like Drip Café are key incubators of the homophobia, transphobia and misogyny that underpin this assault," the group said. articles.title: Colombia’s earthquake tore apart this family with triplets. Only one survived
articles.summary: Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family.
articles.body: Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family. When the 7.4 magnitude earthquake shook western Colombia on August 10, the Saavedra Caycedo family was in their apartment in Cali, one of the hardest-hit cities. Search and rescue efforts at the site began immediately and continued for days. Family and friends took to the streets to ask for help and volunteer in the rescue operations. The triplets, Ana Maria, Sofia and Isabella Saavedra Caycedo; their father Jair Saavedra; their mother Vicky Caycedo and their uncle Diego Caycedo would all be pulled from the debris in the hours and days that followed. The parents were found embracing in their final moments. Sofia and Diego were found dead too. And Isabella’s body was the last to be pulled from the rubble, the triplets’ cousin Camila Martínez Sierra said. A family-organized GoFundMe campaign for Ana Maria has already received thousands of donations. The campaign page says she has already undergone surgery “and now faces a long recovery process.” “Our hearts are broken by the loss of my uncle Jairo and Vicky and my cousins Sofía and Isabella,” Marinez Sierra posted to Instagram on Friday. “Now is the time to stay united and be there for our cousin Ana. Every bit of help, prayer, donation, and sharing counts.” The triplets, according to the family’s fundraising campaign, had recently graduated from university and worked together. “They had dreams, plans, and a whole life ahead of them,” their family wrote on the GoFundMe page. “We want Ana María to have a solid foundation to recover physically and emotionally and to restart her life, without also having to worry about how to pay for everything that is to come.” Martínez Sierra remembered her relatives with several photos and videos of large family gatherings, trips, parties and moments they shared together. One photo shows the family dressed in matching white outfits and black hats, sitting poolside with wide smiles at what appears to be a family reunion. Another shows them gathered around a night-time bonfire. “I can only look at these videos and photos with a heart full of memories and a mix of love, nostalgia, and a pain I still don’t know how to explain,” she wrote in an Instagram post. “Here are our reunions, the laughter, the hugs, the family moments, my uncles, the triplets … moments we lived without imagining that one day we would look at these images in such a different way,” Martínez Sierra said. The Saavedra Caycedo family are among the at least 294 people confirmed to have been killed. Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management said another 320 are missing while nearly 4,000 were injured in the earthquake. More than 12,000 homes have been destroyed and over 100 buildings have been leveled. The earthquake was the deadliest to hit Colombia in decades. Families have been sharing urgent pleas on social media, hoping to track down missing loved ones and rescuers are continuing to work through the rubble. “One never thinks that a photo can become such a precious memory, nor that a hug that seemed so ordinary could become something we would keep forever in our hearts,” Martínez Sierra said. “This earthquake changed our lives in a matter of seconds,” Martínez Sierra said. “It reminded us, in the most painful way, that nothing is guaranteed and that many times we put off a hug, a phone call, an ‘I love you,’ a meeting, a visit.”

articles.title: Sem janelas e mais econômico: como será voar no 'avião-arraia' | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeto da americana JetZero terá telas no lugar das janelas e iluminação natural por claraboias. Empresa diz que formato da aeronave poderá reduzir consumo de combustível em até 50%.
articles.summary: Projeto da americana JetZero terá telas no lugar das janelas e iluminação natural por claraboias. Empresa diz que formato da aeronave poderá reduzir consumo de combustível.
articles.body:
Viajar no avião Z4, projeto da americana JetZero, será bem diferente de voar em um avião comum. Em vez das janelas ao lado dos passageiros, a aeronave terá telas que mostrarão imagens do lado de fora captadas por câmeras de alta definição.

O projeto tem um formato que lembra uma arraia, com a área central integrada às asas . A JetZero diz que o desenho melhora a aerodinâmica e poderá reduzir entre 30% e 50% o consumo de combustível em comparação com modelos como o Boeing 787.

🗒️ Tem alguma sugestão de reportagem? Envie para o g1

A iluminação natural da cabine virá de duas claraboias instaladas próximas às primeiras fileiras. O avião deverá transportar cerca de 250 passageiros, distribuídos em seis seções , e terá um compartimento de bagagem para cada assento.

Críticos ouvidos pelo Wall Street Journal apontam que passageiros próximos às asas poderão sentir mais desconforto nas curvas da aeronave e que a falta de janelas poderá aumentar a sensação de enjoo.

Avião Z4 terá telas no lugar das janelas ao lado dos assentos — Foto: Divulgação/JetZero

Outra mudança do projeto está nas portas: elas serão posicionadas em locais distintos dos usados em aviões convencionais, o que pode dificultar a adaptação do Z4 na maioria dos aeroportos, já que eles estão mais preparados para receber modelos tradicionais.

A JetZero planeja fazer o primeiro voo de um protótipo em escala real em 2027. A empresa pretende iniciar o uso comercial da aeronave no começo da década de 2030.

O Z4 foi projetado para voos de até 5.000 milhas náuticas (cerca de 9.200 km). A autonomia seria suficiente, por exemplo, para uma viagem entre São Paulo e Madri, na Espanha , uma distância de aproximadamente 8.400 km.

A empresa já tem o apoio de companhias aéreas americanas. A United Airlines planeja comprar 200 unidades do Z4 , enquanto Delta e Alaska Airlines também apoiam o projeto.

Para acelerar o desenvolvimento, a JetZero pretende usar componentes presentes em outros aviões e que já foram aprovados pela Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA), órgão que regula o setor no país.

A empresa também tem um acordo de US$ 3 bilhões (R$ 15 bilhões) com o governo americano para financiar a construção de uma fábrica na Carolina do Norte. A estrutura será usada para acelerar a produção da aeronave.

Se o projeto avançar como planejado, o avião-arraia poderá unir uma cabine diferente da convencional com uma promessa de redução significativa no consumo de combustível. Mas, antes de chegar aos passageiros, ele terá que passar por uma série de testes.

articles.title: New satellite images show Europe’s disappearing rivers due to drought
articles.summary: Half of Europe’s land is experiencing drought with rivers running low from the Danube to the Rhine.
articles.body:
Drought conditions have worsened across Central and Western Europe since the start of the summer with southern England, northern Italy and parts of Central Europe among the hardest-hit areas, according to the Global Drought Observatory.

About half of Europe’s land area is experiencing drought with 9 percent reaching the alert level, including southern Germany, Hungary, Romania, Austria, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, according to the Combined Drought Indicator for mid-July.

On Wednesday, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre said the Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube rivers had reached record-low levels after continued hotter and drier conditions.

Al Jazeera’s Open Source Unit analysed satellite imagery showing signs of worsening drought, including retreating water in major rivers, declining soil moisture and the yellowing of green spaces in several cities.

A time-series comparison of satellite images of the Loire River near the French city of Saumur shows a clear change in the shape of the river channel during August from 2023 to 2026.

In images from previous years, larger portions of the channel appear to be covered by water while later comparisons reveal wider islands and larger sandy and gravelly areas within the river.

In an image captured on August 8 this year, substantially larger exposed areas can be seen within the channel compared with the previous images, coinciding with surrounding agricultural areas turning brown and pale.

These visual changes are consistent with the broader picture documented by the Joint Research Centre, which said the Loire had reached record-low levels in August.

Near Moissac in southwestern France, a satellite comparison from May 21 to August 1 shows a considerable change in the colour of farm areas and vegetation surrounding the Garonne River.

In the May image, large areas of fields and vegetation appear in shades of green while the August image shows larger areas in brown and pale shades.

These conditions have occurred during documented hydrological stress in the Garonne basin. In early July, the Garonne River management authority began an early operation to support river levels, describing it as the earliest such intervention since the system was introduced in 1993 after river flows near Toulouse approached record-low levels for that time of year.

In Germany, comparisons of satellite images taken near Kaub show an expansion of exposed sandy and gravelly areas within the Rhine River channel from May 1 to July 29.

In the May image, the channel appears filled with water while the late July image reveals larger exposed areas within the river and along its banks, accompanied by a clear change in the colour of surrounding vegetation and fields.

Rhine water levels in Germany have reached record lows, causing disruptions to shipping. On Wednesday, the Reuters news agency reported that falling water levels had reached unprecedented levels and brought shipping traffic to a halt at a bottleneck on the river with some vessels becoming stranded.

Earlier, Germany’s inland waterway transport sector warned that the severe decline near Kaub could make commercial and tourist navigation impossible on parts of the river. Recent data also showed that vessels were operating with much lighter loads than usual because of reduced available draft.

In Italy, images of the Po River near Boretto in the Emilia-Romagna region show changes in the extent of water and exposed areas during August in 2023 and 2026.

The 2023 image shows a larger water-covered area in parts of the channel while the 2026 image shows sandy and gravelly areas.

This coincides with the Joint Research Centre’s report that the Po basin is experiencing severe hydrological stress while parts of Italy are facing pressure on water use for irrigation and energy production.

The impact of falling water levels is also visible on the Danube, which has experienced declines along several sections in Hungary and Romania.

The Joint Research Centre said reduced Danube flows are putting pressure on navigation, water supplies and agricultural activity as well as the energy sector. Satellite imagery showed a noticeable decline in water levels from August 9, 2025, to August 9, 2026.

In England, satellite imagery captured visible changes across large areas of London, including Hyde Park, and the area around Stonehenge, where vegetation vitality has declined significantly.

England recorded just 6.5mm (a quarter of an inch) of rainfall in July, equivalent to 10 percent of the long-term average, making it the driest July since records began in 1836.

On Tuesday, the United Kingdom’s Environment Agency announced that 71.3 percent of England was officially in drought, including all areas of Greater London, while reservoir storage had fallen to 69 percent.

Satellite images of Hyde Park in central London captured in July 2025 and July 2026 show the scale of the severe drought.

The environmental impact has also extended to green spaces in other major cities. Satellite images of parks in the Austrian capital, Vienna, show changes in grass colour and water availability and the effects of extreme heat.

European monitoring centres expect dry conditions to continue through September.

High-resolution satellite imagery from SkySat shows a striking visual change in the vitality of vegetation at Auer-Welsbach Park in Vienna between the summers of 2025 and 2026.

In an image captured on July 22, 2025, the park appears to have dark-green grassy areas complemented by lush tree cover. By contrast, the image captured on July 28, 2026, shows extensive yellowing and a severe decline in greenery, with most of the park’s open grassy areas turning brown and pale.

This visual decline documents the arrival of water and heat stress at the heart of European cities where extreme temperatures and a lack of rainfall have caused soil to dry out and public green spaces to deteriorate in Britain, Austria and other parts of Central Europe.

articles.title: CBS News correspondent accused of sexual harassment in former ABC producer's lawsuit
articles.summary: Samira Said's lawsuit alleges Matt Gutman made sexualized comments and ABC denied her medical accommodations after covering the Uvalde school shooting.
articles.body: Former ABC News field producer Samira Said sued CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman, ABC News, The Walt Disney Co. and an ABC bureau chief on Friday, alleging Gutman made sexualized workplace comments and ABC later fired her after denying medical accommodations related to trauma from covering the Uvalde school massacre. Said alleged Gutman initiated a conversation about another female correspondent while Said worked on an otherwise all-male team, according to the complaint filed In Los Angeles Superior Court. "While the team waited in a public queue during the assignment, Gutman initiated a discussion rating a female correspondent’s appearance and reducing her professional standing to a numerical score based on her physical attributes," the complaint said. BATTLE BETWEEN BARI WEISS AND ‘60 MINUTES’ EXPLODES AS SCOTT PELLEY ACCUSES HER OF MURDERING THE SHOW "The male crew joined in, continuing to assess the woman’s body and looks in Said’s presence. The men attempted to draw Said into the conversation by soliciting her views. Said declined and stated the conversation was inappropriate." The filing described a second alleged incident during a movie-release press event, when Said and Gutman disagreed over whether their team should leave the work site. "In front of multiple coworkers, Gutman responded by making a sexualized insinuation that Said must have an after-hours date in the city and that this is why she did not want to relocate," the complaint said. "The remark, made audibly to others, demeaned Said and reduced her professional judgment to a sexualized stereotype." The allegations against Gutman are part of a broader lawsuit in which Said accused ABC and Disney of discrimination, retaliation, failing to accommodate her medical conditions and wrongfully terminating her. Said worked in ABC News' Los Angeles bureau from May 2021 until March 2025, according to The Hollywood Reporter. BARI WEISS POACHES CONSERVATIVE NY TIMES COLUMNIST, OTHERS JOIN '60 MINUTES' IN CBS PROGRAM SHAKEUP Said alleged she was experiencing COVID-19 symptoms when management urged her to cover the May 2022 mass school shooting in Uvalde, Texas. Her assignment included interviewing children who witnessed their classmates and teachers being killed, after which she said she experienced severe psychological symptoms, the lawsuit states. A psychiatrist later cleared Said to return from medical leave with accommodations, but she alleged then-Los Angeles bureau chief David Herndon would not permit a restricted schedule. Herndon "made it clear that unless she returned without restrictions and with full-week availability, she would not be permitted to resume her role," the complaint said. Said alleged she was subsequently moved to weekend desk shifts. She was later assigned to cover the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires and other hazardous weather events in the city, during which, the complain alleges, heavy equipment allegedly struck her foot and caused a bone contusion. PARAMOUNT ESCALATES THREAT TO LEAVE CALIFORNIA AS DEM AG'S ANTITRUST LAWSUIT STALLS WARNER BROS MERGER ABC terminated Said during what had been presented as a routine meeting on March 5, 2025, the filing said. She is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, attorneys’ fees and a jury trial. The allegations have not been adjudicated. Gutman joined CBS in January after 17 years at ABC and became the first major on-air hire under CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. CBS announced that Gutman would report for "CBS Mornings" and the "CBS Evening News," lead reporting for "48 Hours," contribute to "60 Minutes" and serve as a fill-in anchor. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Weiss praised Gutman’s reporting when CBS announced his hiring. "Matt Gutman goes there," Weiss said. "He brings the audience along with him to whatever story he is covering, and he approaches his work with the qualities we look for in all our journalists: fearlessness, energy and relentlessness."
